title: Water
summary: Why water is the medium of life: how polar molecules and hydrogen bonds give water its cohesive, adhesive, solvent and thermal properties, and what that means for living things.

keyterms.definition: A covalent bond in which electrons are shared unequally, so one atom (oxygen in water) carries a partial negative charge and the other (hydrogen) a partial positive charge.
A weak attraction between a partially positive hydrogen atom of one polar molecule and a partially negative atom (such as oxygen) of another.
Attraction between water molecules due to hydrogen bonding, so water molecules stick to each other.
Attraction between water molecules and other polar or charged materials, due to hydrogen bonds or other intermolecular attractions.
Resistance of a water surface to being broken, caused by cohesion between surface water molecules; allows some organisms to live on the water surface.
Movement of water through narrow spaces, such as soil pores or plant cell walls, caused by adhesion to the surfaces combined with cohesion.
A liquid in which solutes dissolve; water dissolves many polar and charged substances, making it the medium for metabolism and transport.
Describes polar or charged substances that are attracted to water and dissolve in it, e.g. glucose, amino acids and ions.
Describes non-polar substances that are not attracted to water and are insoluble in it, e.g. lipids such as fats and oils.
Energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C; high in water because hydrogen bonds must be broken.
The upward force exerted by a fluid on an object in it; much greater in water than in air because water is much denser.
A fluid's resistance to flow; water is far more viscous than air, so moving through water requires more energy.
The rate at which a substance conducts heat; water conducts heat much faster than air, so animals lose heat faster in water.
The habitable zone around a star where temperatures allow water to exist as a liquid on a planet's surface.

questions.prompt: Why is a water molecule polar?
options: Oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen, so O is partially negative and H partially positive
Water molecules carry a net negative charge because oxygen gains an electron
Hydrogen and oxygen share electrons equally but the molecule is bent
Hydrogen bonds inside the molecule hold the atoms in place
questions.explanation: Oxygen is more electronegative, so electrons in the O–H covalent bonds are shared unequally, giving partial charges. The molecule has no net charge, and hydrogen bonds form between molecules, not within one.

questions.statement: Hydrogen bonds in water form between atoms within a single water molecule.
questions.explanation: Within a water molecule the atoms are joined by polar covalent bonds. Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular: they form between the partially positive H of one molecule and the partially negative O of another.

questions.text: The attraction of water molecules to each other through hydrogen bonding is called ___.
questions.explanation: Cohesion is water sticking to water. Adhesion is water sticking to other polar or charged materials.

questions.prompt: Water can be pulled up a xylem vessel as a continuous column under tension without the column breaking. Which property of water explains this?
options: Adhesion to lignin in the xylem wall
High specific heat capacity
Cohesion between water molecules
Water's ability to dissolve mineral ions
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules (cohesion) let the column withstand tension as water is pulled up from the leaves. Adhesion helps, but it is cohesion that stops the column snapping.

questions.statement: Surface tension allows some small animals, such as pond skaters, to use the water surface as a habitat.
questions.explanation: Cohesion between water molecules at the surface creates surface tension, which can support the weight of small organisms without the surface breaking.

questions.text: Water moves through narrow pores in soil and through plant cell walls by ___ action.
questions.explanation: Capillary action results from adhesion of water to the polar surfaces (e.g. cellulose in cell walls) combined with cohesion pulling more water along.

questions.prompt: Match each term to the correct description.

pairs.right: Unequal sharing of electrons between O and H
Attraction between δ+ H and δ− O of different molecules
Water molecules attracted to other water molecules
Water attracted to polar or charged surfaces

questions.explanation: Polar covalent bonds within each molecule create the partial charges that allow hydrogen bonds between molecules; hydrogen bonds then cause both cohesion and adhesion.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to explain how water's structure leads to cohesion.
items: Oxygen attracts shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen
Oxygen gains a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge
δ+ hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to δ− oxygen of another
Hydrogen bonds hold many water molecules together
questions.explanation: Unequal sharing of electrons creates partial charges; opposite partial charges on neighbouring molecules attract, forming hydrogen bonds, which collectively produce cohesion.

questions.prompt: Why is water described as the medium for life?
options: Because all organisms live in water
Because the first cells originated in water and most processes of life still occur in water
Because water is the most abundant molecule in the atmosphere
Because water molecules are used as an energy source by cells
questions.explanation: The first cells arose in water and cytoplasm is mainly water, so most metabolic reactions take place in aqueous solution. Many organisms live on land, and water is not an energy source.

questions.prompt: An individual hydrogen bond is weak. Why do hydrogen bonds still have such large effects on the properties of water?
options: They are stronger than covalent bonds
Each water molecule can only form one hydrogen bond
They only form when water is frozen
There are very large numbers of them, so collectively they are strong
questions.explanation: Each water molecule can form hydrogen bonds with several neighbours. Although each bond is weak and constantly breaking and reforming, their vast number gives water its cohesive and thermal properties.

Sodium ions
Triglyceride (fat)
Amino acids
questions.explanation: Fats are non-polar, so they are not attracted to water and do not dissolve. Glucose, ions and amino acids are polar or charged and therefore hydrophilic.

questions.statement: Most enzymes catalyse reactions in aqueous solution, which is why water is described as the medium for metabolism.
questions.explanation: Substrates and enzymes dissolved in water can move and collide, so the cytoplasm acts as the medium in which most metabolic reactions occur.

questions.text: Polar and charged substances that dissolve in water are described as ___.
questions.explanation: Hydrophilic means 'water-loving': polar or charged particles form attractions with water molecules and so dissolve.

questions.statement: Being hydrophobic is always a disadvantage for molecules in cells.
questions.explanation: Some functions depend on insolubility: hydrophobic phospholipid tails form the core of membranes, and insoluble fats make compact energy stores.

questions.prompt: Why does water have a high specific heat capacity?
options: Hydrogen bonds must be broken before water molecules can move faster
Water molecules are very large and heavy
Water is a poor conductor of heat
Water contains dissolved ions that absorb heat
questions.explanation: Much of the energy supplied to water is used to break hydrogen bonds rather than raise temperature, so water heats up and cools down slowly, giving aquatic habitats stable temperatures.

questions.text: Water conducts heat much faster than air, so it has a higher thermal ___.
questions.explanation: Thermal conductivity is the rate heat is conducted. Animals in water such as the ringed seal lose body heat quickly, so need insulation like blubber.

questions.prompt: Match each property of water (compared with air) to a consequence for aquatic animals.

pairs.right: Body is supported, so less skeletal support needed
Streamlined shape reduces energy cost of swimming
Heat lost quickly; insulation such as blubber needed

questions.explanation: Water is denser, more viscous, conducts heat faster and has a higher specific heat capacity than air; each property shapes adaptations of aquatic animals.

questions.prompt: The ringed seal (Pusa hispida) lives in Arctic waters. Which adaptation most directly counters the high thermal conductivity of water?
options: Streamlined body shape
Large lungs for buoyancy control
Flippers for propulsion
A thick layer of blubber under the skin
questions.explanation: Water conducts heat away from the body far faster than air. Blubber is an insulating fat layer that reduces this heat loss; streamlining deals with viscosity, not heat.

questions.prompt: The black-throated loon (Gavia arctica) flies in air but dives underwater to catch fish. Which statement best contrasts the two media?
options: Air provides more buoyancy, so flying needs less energy than swimming
Water is more viscous and more buoyant than air, so diving needs a streamlined body and effort to overcome buoyancy
Water has a lower specific heat capacity than air, so the loon heats up underwater
Air is more viscous, so the loon swims faster than it flies
questions.explanation: Water is denser (more buoyant) and more viscous than air. A diving bird must push against high drag and buoyancy, while in air it must generate lift because air gives almost no support.

questions.statement: Water's solvent properties allow it to act as a transport medium, e.g. in blood plasma and in xylem sap.
questions.explanation: Hydrophilic substances such as glucose, amino acids and mineral ions dissolve in water and are carried in solution in blood plasma and in xylem and phloem.

questions.prompt: What is the leading hypothesis for the origin of much of Earth's water?
options: It was produced by photosynthesis in the first cells
It was delivered by collisions with asteroids (and possibly comets) from outside Earth
It formed from oxygen released by volcanoes reacting with hydrogen in the modern atmosphere
It was released when ice caps melted at the end of the last ice age
questions.explanation: Earth's water is thought to have an extraplanetary origin, delivered by water-bearing asteroids colliding with the young Earth. Photosynthesis appeared much later and does not produce water in net terms.

questions.statement: Earth has retained its water partly because its gravity is strong enough to hold an atmosphere.
questions.explanation: Earth's gravity prevents water vapour escaping into space, and its atmosphere and distance from the Sun keep temperatures in the range where water is mainly liquid.

questions.text: The region around a star where a planet could have liquid surface water is called the ___ zone.
questions.explanation: The Goldilocks (habitable) zone is 'not too hot, not too cold' for liquid water, so it is the focus of searches for extraterrestrial life.

questions.prompt: Why does the search for extraterrestrial life focus on planets where liquid water may be present?
options: Because water is the only molecule that contains hydrogen
Because water produces oxygen for respiration
Because life as we know it requires liquid water as a solvent and medium for metabolism
Because planets with water must already have life
questions.explanation: All known life depends on liquid water as the medium for metabolism, so liquid water is regarded as a requirement for life. Water does not guarantee life is present.

questions.statement: A planet that has liquid water must have life.
questions.explanation: Liquid water is considered necessary for life as we know it, but not sufficient; many other conditions are required.

questions.prompt: Match each factor to how it affects water on a planet.

pairs.right: Holds water vapour and atmosphere near the planet

questions.explanation: Liquid water requires both a source of water and conditions (gravity, temperature set by distance from the star) that let it remain as liquid.

questions.prompt: Which feature of Earth best explains why its water is mostly liquid rather than ice or vapour?
options: Its distance from the Sun keeps temperatures between 0 °C and 100 °C over most of the surface
Its magnetic field heats the oceans
Its large moon pulls water into tides
Its oceans contain dissolved salt which prevents freezing everywhere
questions.explanation: Earth lies within the Sun's Goldilocks zone, so surface temperatures mostly keep water liquid. Salt lowers the freezing point slightly but is not the main explanation.

questions.text: Water vapour would escape into space from a planet with too little ___.
questions.explanation: A planet needs sufficient mass (and so gravity) to retain an atmosphere and the water within it.

questions.prompt: Put these events in order in the hypothesis for how Earth came to have liquid water oceans.
items: Young Earth forms, hot and largely dry
Earth's gravity retains water vapour in the atmosphere
Earth cools and water vapour condenses into liquid oceans
questions.explanation: Water is thought to have been delivered after Earth formed, retained by gravity, then condensed as the planet cooled into the temperature range for liquid water.

questions.prompt: Which property of liquid water makes it especially important for any possible life on other planets?
options: It is non-polar, so it dissolves fats
It has a low specific heat capacity, so temperatures change quickly
It is less viscous than air
It is a solvent for many polar substances, allowing metabolic reactions in solution
questions.explanation: Water's polarity makes it an excellent solvent so reactants can meet in solution. It is polar, has a high specific heat capacity and is more viscous than air.
